- ✓ **D. Folder Creator (correct):** the Organization Administrator role is limited to managing access, so folder creation needs a separate role such as Folder Creator (or Folder Admin) granted on the organization.

## Key idea
Organization Administrator manages IAM, not resources: grant Folder Creator or Folder Admin to anyone who must build the folder structure.
Q008194:
## Organization, folders, projects
The Google Cloud resource hierarchy has the **organization** at the root, optional **folders** for grouping, and **projects** that hold the actual resources (VMs, buckets, databases). Every resource except the organization has exactly one parent.
- Folders can contain projects and other folders, nested up to **10 levels**, with up to 300 direct child folders per folder.
- Folders model departments, teams or legal entities, and can model environments below them.
- Allow policies, deny policies and organization policies attached to a node apply to everything below it.
## Delegation with folders
Granting a department head an admin role on the department folder gives them control of every project created in that folder and nothing outside it. Guardrails such as organization policies set once at the organization reach every folder and project.
## Why not several organizations
Google recommends folders under one organization for most cases. Multiple organizations mean no central visibility by default, and common policies have to be copied into each one.
## Example
`organizations/1234` -> `folders/News` -> `folders/News-prod` -> `projects/news-web-prod`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Department folders with environment subfolders (correct):** each head gets an admin role on one folder subtree, while organization-level policies give the security team one place to set guardrails for all departments.
- ✗ **B. One project per department with labels:** labels don't create a permission boundary, so dev and prod resources share the same IAM policy and the Owner role on a shared project is far more than least privilege.
- ✗ **C. Folders inside projects:** projects are the lowest container and can't hold folders; folders always sit above projects in the hierarchy.
- ✗ **D. One organization per department:** this removes central control, forces the security team to duplicate every guardrail three times, and is the pattern Google suggests only for fully isolated entities.

## Key idea
Model departments and environments with nested folders under one organization and grant roles on the folder each team owns.
Q008195:
## Creating a project from the CLI
`gcloud projects create PROJECT_ID` creates a project. To place it in the hierarchy, add **one** parent flag:
- `--organization=ORGANIZATION_ID` puts it directly under the organization.
- `--folder=FOLDER_ID` puts it inside a folder.
A resource has exactly one parent, so you use one flag or the other, and the ID you pass must be of that type: a folder ID goes with `--folder`, an organization ID with `--organization`.
## Project ID rules
The project ID is globally unique and **permanent** after creation. It must:
- be 6 to 30 characters long
- start with a lowercase letter
- contain only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens (and not end with a hyphen)
- avoid restricted strings such as `google` or `ssl`
The project **name** (display name) is different: it can contain spaces and capitals and can be changed later.
## Example
`gcloud projects create acme-payments-dev --folder=834512776120` creates the project with ID `acme-payments-dev` as a child of that folder.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. folders create:** this command creates a folder, not a project; the payments team would get a subfolder and still no project to hold resources.
- ✗ **B. Folder ID passed as --organization:** 834512776120 is a folder ID, so `--organization` points at an organization that doesn't exist (or isn't the intended parent) instead of placing the project in the folder.
- ✓ **C. projects create with --folder (correct):** the ID uses only lowercase letters and hyphens, starts with a letter, and the single `--folder` flag sets the parent folder.
- ✗ **D. Capitals and underscores:** project IDs must start with a lowercase letter and may only contain lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, so this ID is rejected.

## Key idea
Use `gcloud projects create ID --folder=FOLDER_ID` (or `--organization`), with a lowercase, permanent project ID.
Q008196:
## A migration changes the parent, not the data
Moving a project between organizations updates the project's **parent** in the resource hierarchy. It is not a data copy: VMs, buckets and databases stay online with no downtime.
## What stays and what changes
- **Stays the same**: project ID and number, the data and resources, roles granted **directly on the project**, project-level quotas, and the **billing account** link.
- **Changes**: roles **inherited** from the source organization or folders are lost; the source organization policies are replaced by the destination's; inherited organization-level quotas are lost.
## Things to prepare
- Custom roles defined at the source organization don't exist in the destination; recreate them first.
- Discounts and support tiers of the source organization might not carry over.
- Cloud Asset Inventory can take a few days to show the full resource list after the move.
## Example
A group had Compute Admin on the acquired company's `folders/eng`. After the move, that group has no access to the project unless the destination grants it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Inherited roles lost (correct):** roles from the source organization or folders came from the old ancestors, so they stop applying once the project has a new parent; only roles granted directly on the project move with it.
- ✗ **B. Automatic billing relink:** the project stays linked to its original billing account; changing billing is a separate post-migration step.
- ✗ **C. New project ID:** the project ID and project number stay the same, so API keys, scripts and resource names keep working.
- ✗ **D. Resources stopped:** migration is a metadata change to the parent, and services, VMs and databases keep running throughout.
- ✓ **E. Destination organization policies (correct):** organization policies are inherited from ancestors, so the destination organization and folder constraints replace the source ones immediately.

## Key idea
Moving a project keeps its ID, resources, direct roles and billing link, but swaps everything it inherits: IAM roles and organization policies.
Q008197:
## Default grants on a new organization
When an organization resource is created, its initial allow policy grants two roles to the **entire domain** at the organization level:
- Project Creator (`roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator`)
- Billing Account Creator (`roles/billing.creator`)
This keeps existing users working without disruption when the organization appears. Nothing else is created.
## Taking control
Once the Organization Administrator is ready to lock things down, they remove these organization-level grants and grant narrower access instead, for example Project Creator only to a platform group, or roles on specific folders. Because allow policies are inherited, a grant to the whole domain at the organization lets everyone create projects anywhere below it.
## Example
`gcloud organizations remove-iam-policy-binding 1234 --member="domain:example.com" --role="roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator"`, then `gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding 1234 --member="group:platform-team@example.com" --role="roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator"`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Remove Billing Account Creator:** creating billing accounts and creating projects are separate permissions, so the domain would still hold Project Creator.
- ✓ **B. Replace the domain grant (correct):** the ability to create projects comes from the default Project Creator binding for the whole domain, so removing it and granting the role to the group limits creation to the platform team.
- ✗ **C. Remove project Owner roles:** owning an existing project doesn't let a user create new projects; the permission comes from Project Creator on the organization.
- ✗ **D. Organization Administrator for the group:** this role manages IAM and does not even include project creation, and it would also give the group far more control than needed.

## Key idea
A new organization grants Project Creator and Billing Account Creator to the whole domain; remove those grants and give narrower ones when you take control.
Q008198:
## The resource locations constraint
`constraints/gcp.resourceLocations` is a list constraint that defines where **location-based** resources can be created. By default, resources can be created anywhere.
## Value groups
Google curates **value groups**, collections of locations used with the `in:` prefix:
- `in:eu-locations`: all EU locations
- `in:us-locations`: all locations within the US
- `in:us-east1-locations`: one region and its zones
A value group grows automatically when Google adds a location, so the policy covers future regions without edits. Google recommends value groups.
## Multi-region values are not groups
Allowing or denying a multi-region such as `eu` or `us` applies only to multi-region resources (for example some storage services). It doesn't include the regions inside it: denying `us` still allows `us-east1`.
## Example policy
```
name: organizations/1234/policies/gcp.resourceLocations
spec:
rules:
- values:
allowedValues:
- in:eu-locations
```

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. IAM deny on locations:** IAM decides who may call an API, not where a resource may be created; location rules are the job of an organization policy constraint.
- ✗ **B. Plain eu value:** a multi-region value only covers multi-region resources; it does not imply the regions inside it, so regional resources in EU regions would be blocked.
- ✗ **C. External IP constraint:** `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` controls which VMs may have external IPv4 addresses and has nothing to do with resource location.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** in:eu-locations value group: the `in:` prefix with the curated EU group allows every EU region, zone and multi-region now and in the future, and implicitly denies everything else.

## Key idea
Restrict locations with `gcp.resourceLocations` and `in:` value groups such as `in:eu-locations`, not with multi-region names.
Q008199:
## Google Cloud security baseline
Organizations created on or after **May 3, 2024** get a bundle of organization policies enforced automatically at creation (the security baseline). Examples:
- `iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` (Domain restricted sharing): only identities from allowed organizations or Workspace customer IDs can be added to IAM policies.
- `iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`: no new service account keys.
- `storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess`: no per-object ACLs.
## Domain restricted sharing
The constraint lists the principal sets or Google Workspace customer IDs whose principals may be added to allow policies. Everyone else, including personal `gmail.com` accounts, is rejected when someone tries to add them.
## Viewer is a legacy basic role
IAM's basic roles are now Admin (`roles/admin`), Writer (`roles/writer`) and Reader (`roles/reader`). Viewer (`roles/viewer`), Editor and Owner are **legacy basic roles**, which existed before IAM. Role bindings for legacy basic roles can't carry IAM Conditions; the newer basic roles can.
## Checking and changing it
- `gcloud resource-manager org-policies list --organization=ORGANIZATION_ID` shows which constraints are set.
- An Organization Policy Administrator can add the partner's customer ID, or create a project-level exception, if sharing with outsiders is truly needed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Binding limit:** the error names a disallowed customer, not a policy size limit, and a project with a few bindings is nowhere near the size limit.
- ✓ **B. Security baseline domain restriction (correct):** an organization created after May 2024 enforces Domain restricted sharing by default, which blocks adding principals from other domains such as personal Gmail accounts to IAM policies.
- ✗ **C. Legacy basic role restriction:** IAM has no rule tying legacy basic roles to the grantee's domain, and bindings for legacy basic roles such as Viewer can't carry IAM Conditions at all, so a condition is no workaround either.
- ✗ **D. Cloud Identity invitation:** IAM accepts any Google account unless an organization policy restricts it; joining the company domain is not a general requirement.

## Key idea
New organizations enforce baseline constraints such as Domain restricted sharing; check organization policies when outside identities are rejected.
Q008200:
## How list constraints are evaluated
A policy set on a resource replaces its parent's policy **unless** it sets `inheritFromParent: true`. With inheritance on, the parent's effective policy and the child's policy are **merged and reconciled**.
## Deny wins
For constraints with list rules, a `DENY` value always takes precedence during reconciliation. If a folder denies `projects/123` and a project below it allows `projects/123`, the effective policy still denies it. Google recommends not listing the same value in both allowed and denied lists, because the result is hard to read.
## Getting an exception
To let one project use the value, the project's policy would have to stop inheriting (`inheritFromParent: false`) and set its own values, or the folder policy has to change.
## Example
- Folder denies `projects/legacy-images`.
- Project inherits and allows `projects/legacy-images`.
- Effective policy at the project: `projects/legacy-images` denied.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Projects can only add denies:** a project can override an inherited list policy by setting `inheritFromParent: false`, so this limit doesn't exist.
- ✗ **B. 24-hour propagation:** there is no day-long replacement delay; the result is the documented merge outcome, not a timing issue.
- ✓ **C. Merged list with deny precedence (correct):** because the project inherits, its allow is merged with the folder's deny, and a denied value always beats an allowed one for list rules.
- ✗ **D. under:** prefix needed: `compute.trustedImageProjects` supports only the `is:` prefix and takes values in the form `projects/PROJECT_ID`, so the plain path is valid; the cause is the deny precedence.

## Key idea
For list constraints with inheritance, values are merged and DENY always wins; stop inheriting to make a real exception.
Q008201:
## Boolean rules don't merge
A constraint with a boolean rule is either enforced or not enforced. Unlike list rules, boolean rules are **not merged and reconciled** across the hierarchy: if a policy is specified on a resource, that resource's `true` or `false` value decides the effective policy.
## Example from the docs
- A folder sets `enforced: true`.
- A project below it sets `enforced: false`.
- The folder's value is ignored for that project, and the constraint is **not enforced** there.
## Keeping guardrails in place
Only principals with Organization Policy Administrator (`roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin`) can set policies, so limiting that role is how you stop projects from overriding a folder. `gcloud org-policies describe CONSTRAINT --project=PROJECT_ID --effective` shows what is actually applied.
## Not retroactive
Separately, new policies generally don't change existing resources; but here the VMs were created after the folder policy, so the project-level override is the explanation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Project-level override (correct):** the project's own policy for the boolean constraint sets enforce to false, and a boolean value on a resource replaces the inherited value instead of merging with it.
- ✗ **B. Service accounts exempt:** constraints are enforced by the service on the API request, whoever the caller is, including service accounts and the CLI.
- ✗ **C. Only new projects covered:** inheritance applies to all descendants of the folder, existing or new; the age of the project is not the deciding factor.
- ✗ **D. Merging ancestors:** that is how list rules with inheritance behave; boolean rules use the policy closest to the resource when one is set there.

## Key idea
For boolean constraints, a policy set on the project wins outright; restrict who holds Organization Policy Administrator to keep folder guardrails.
Q008202:
## Organization policies prevent, they don't clean up
Google Cloud services enforce constraints when resources are created or updated. The application of a new organization policy is **usually not retroactive**: if a resource is already in a state that the new policy forbids, it is in violation, but the service keeps working as before. Google designed it this way so a new policy can't shut down a running business.
## Resource locations specifically
The docs say the resource locations constraint restricts resource **creation**; it helps prevent violations but does not identify or remediate existing ones. To find them, use tools such as Security Health Analytics in Security Command Center or Cloud Asset Inventory searches, then move or recreate the resources yourself.
## Testing first
Google advises testing a new location policy on non-production folders and rolling it out gradually, and dry-run mode can log violations before enforcement.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Uniform bucket-level access exemption:** uniform bucket-level access only switches a bucket from object ACLs to IAM; it doesn't exempt the bucket from organization policies.
- ✓ **B. Not retroactive (correct):** the location constraint is checked when resources are created, so existing buckets are violations that keep running until someone remediates them.
- ✗ **C. 72-hour propagation and deletion:** no organization policy deletes existing resources, and there is no multi-day delay that ends in deletion.
- ✗ **D. Compute Engine only:** the resource locations constraint covers many location-based services, Cloud Storage buckets included.

## Key idea
New organization policies stop future violations; existing non-compliant resources must be found and fixed separately.
Q008203:
## Dry-run mode
An organization policy can be created in **dry-run mode**, in active (enforced) mode, or both. In dry-run mode the policy is evaluated like an enforced one and **violations are written to audit logs**, but the violating actions are **not denied**.
This lets you watch how a change would affect real workflows before you enforce it.
## Other tools and what they do
- `gcloud org-policies describe CONSTRAINT --effective` shows the effective policy at a resource after inheritance; it doesn't simulate API calls.
- `inheritFromParent` controls whether a child merges its parent's list policy; it has nothing to do with logging.
## Example rollout
1. Set the managed constraint `compute.managed.vmExternalIpAccess` (enforced) as a dry-run policy at the organization. Dry-run mode accepts custom and managed constraints but only a few legacy constraints, so the legacy `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` list constraint can't be used here.
2. Review the audit log entries for a few weeks and fix or except the workloads that need external IPs.
3. Enforce the policy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. inheritFromParent false:** this only stops merging with the parent's policy; it doesn't create a logging-only grace period.
- ✗ **B. describe --effective:** it shows how policies combine at a resource, not which API calls would be rejected by a policy that isn't in place yet.
- ✗ **C. Organization Policy Viewer emails:** a viewer role lets people read policies; no role sends teams lists of violating resources.
- ✓ **D. Dry-run mode (correct):** the policy is evaluated and violations are audit-logged while nothing is denied, which is exactly the "see what breaks first" requirement.

## Key idea
Use dry-run mode to log the violations of a new organization policy before you enforce it.
Q008204:
## IAM answers "who", Organization Policy answers "what"
- **IAM** authorizes **who** can act on which resources, based on permissions in roles.
- **Organization Policy** restricts **what** configurations are allowed on resources, for everyone, regardless of their roles.
A project Owner has every permission in the project, so IAM alone can't stop an Owner from choosing an external IP. An organization policy can.
## Owner is a legacy basic role
Owner (`roles/owner`), Editor and Viewer are IAM's **legacy basic roles**; the current basic roles are Admin (`roles/admin`), Writer (`roles/writer`) and Reader (`roles/reader`). Role bindings for legacy basic roles can't carry IAM Conditions, so the Owner grant can't be narrowed with a condition.
## The external IP constraint
`constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess` is a list constraint naming the VM instances (`projects/PROJECT_ID/zones/ZONE/instances/INSTANCE`) that may use external IPv4 addresses. A policy that denies all values means no VM may have one. It doesn't restrict IPv6 addresses.
## Where to set it
Setting it at the organization makes every folder and project inherit it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Remove Instance Admin:** Owners keep full permissions and can still create VMs with external IPs, so the requirement fails for exactly the group it names.
- ✗ **B. Deny-all egress firewall rule:** VMs still receive external addresses; the rule blocks traffic, not the IP assignment, and Owners can delete the rule.
- ✓ **C. Organization policy on external IPs (correct):** the constraint restricts the VM configuration itself, so the Compute Engine API rejects external IPv4 addresses whoever makes the request, project Owners included.
- ✗ **D. IAM Condition on Owner:** Owner is a legacy basic role, and IAM doesn't accept conditions on role bindings for legacy basic roles; even where conditions are allowed, they can't inspect a VM's requested network configuration.

## Key idea
Use organization policy constraints to restrict resource configuration for everyone; use IAM to decide who can act.
Q008205:
## Granting a role on a project
Access to a project is defined in the project's **allow policy**, a list of role bindings. Each binding links principals to one role, and the role applies to the project and every resource inside it.
## The add command
`gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member=PRINCIPAL --role=ROLE` adds one binding and leaves the rest of the policy as it is.
- `--member` needs a type prefix: `user:`, `group:`, `serviceAccount:` or `domain:`.
- `--role` needs the full role name, such as `roles/viewer` or `roles/logging.viewer`; custom roles use `projects/PROJECT_ID/roles/ROLE_ID` or `organizations/ORG_ID/roles/ROLE_ID`.
## set-iam-policy is different
`gcloud projects set-iam-policy PROJECT_ID policy.json` replaces the **whole** policy with the contents of a file. It takes no `--member` or `--role` flags and can remove existing grants if the file is incomplete.
## Basic and legacy basic roles
`roles/viewer` (Viewer) is a **legacy basic role** that gives broad read access. The current basic roles are Admin (`roles/admin`), Writer (`roles/writer`) and Reader (`roles/reader`); Reader gives similar broad read-only access and, unlike Viewer, its bindings can carry IAM Conditions. For production, predefined roles are preferred where they fit; the grant mechanics are the same for every role.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. user:** prefix for a group: the principal type must match the identity; a group address with `user:` doesn't identify the group and the grant fails or targets the wrong principal.
- ✗ **B. set-iam-policy:** this command replaces the entire policy from a JSON or YAML file; it doesn't take member and role flags and risks wiping existing grants.
- ✗ **C. Short role name:** the role must be given as its full name such as `roles/viewer`; a bare `viewer` isn't a valid role identifier.
- ✓ **D. add-iam-policy-binding with group (correct):** prefix: it adds one binding for the group with the full role name and keeps all other bindings unchanged.

## Key idea
Grant project roles with `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT --member=group:... --role=roles/...`; `set-iam-policy` replaces the whole policy.
Q008206:
## Two separate jobs: provisioning and authentication
When Active Directory stays the identity source for Google Cloud, Google's reference architecture splits the work in two:
- **Provisioning** with **Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS)**, a free Google tool. GCDS queries the LDAP directory and uses the Directory API to add, modify or delete users and groups in Cloud Identity or Google Workspace. It is usually run on premises as a **scheduled task** for continuous provisioning, with a dedicated admin user.
- **Single sign-on** with **SAML**: Cloud Identity delegates authentication to Active Directory (for example through AD FS), so only AD manages credentials and its MFA and password policies apply.
## One-way, no passwords
Provisioning is **one way**: changes in Active Directory are replicated to Google Cloud, never the other way. Provisioning doesn't include passwords; with federation, AD remains the only place credentials live. A user must be provisioned before SSO can succeed.
## Manual management
Users and groups can also be created by hand in the Admin console or the Google Cloud console Groups page, which suits small teams but not an HR-driven directory.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Password hashes back to AD:** provisioning is one way, from AD to Google, and doesn't include passwords; AD stays the only system that manages credentials.
- ✓ **B. SAML SSO to Active Directory (correct):** sign-in is delegated to AD, so users authenticate with their AD passwords and no password is stored in Google.
- ✗ **C. Manual creation:** this neither stays in step with HR changes nor uses AD credentials; it creates a second password to manage.
- ✗ **D. Cloud Identity authoritative:** in this design Active Directory is the authoritative source and changes flow from AD to Cloud Identity, not back.
- ✓ **E. GCDS as a scheduled task (correct):** GCDS reads users and groups from AD over LDAP and keeps Cloud Identity in sync automatically on each run.

## Key idea
Provision with GCDS (one way, AD to Cloud Identity, no passwords) and authenticate with SAML SSO to Active Directory.
Q008207:
## Manage people through groups
Google groups help manage users at scale: every member of a group inherits the IAM roles granted to the group. Adding or removing a person from the group changes their access on every project where the group has roles, with no IAM change.
## The memberships command
`gcloud identity groups memberships add --group-email=GROUP --member-email=MEMBER` adds a user or group to an existing group (Cloud Identity API).
- `--expiration` is an optional duration from now, such as `30d`, `6m` or `3y`, after which the membership expires.
- `--roles` sets the member's role **inside the group** (for example `MEMBER`, `MANAGER`, `OWNER`); it defaults to `MEMBER`.
## Example
`gcloud identity groups memberships add --group-email="gcp-analysts@example.com" --member-email="lee@example.com" --expiration="30d"` gives Lee the group's access for 30 days.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. memberships add with --expiration (correct):** it puts the contractor into the existing group, so he inherits its roles, and the `30d` duration ends the membership automatically.
- ✗ **B. groups create:** the group already exists, and `groups create` doesn't add members or take an expiration.
- ✗ **C. Swapped emails:** the group and member addresses are reversed, and `--roles` sets a role inside the group such as `MEMBER`, not an expiry.
- ✗ **D. Project binding with --expiration:** `add-iam-policy-binding` has no `--expiration` flag (time limits on bindings use IAM Conditions), and this binds the group, not the contractor.

## Key idea
Grant roles to groups and manage people through membership; `gcloud identity groups memberships add --expiration` makes a membership temporary.
Q008208:
## Groups live in the identity system
Google groups belong to the organization's Google Workspace or Cloud Identity account, not to a Google Cloud project. You can create and manage them from the Google Cloud console **Groups** page, from Google Groups, the Admin console or the gcloud CLI.
## Two kinds of permission
- **Group permissions** (create, view, edit, delete groups) are **managed by Google Workspace or Cloud Identity**, not IAM. A Workspace or Cloud Identity administrator grants them through admin privileges or organization-wide group settings.
- **IAM permissions** are needed only to use the console page: Organization Viewer on the organization, plus Logs Viewer to see group membership change logs.
## Example
A user with Organization Viewer and project Owner can open the Groups page and see groups she has access to, but the Create action fails until a Cloud Identity administrator gives her group-management privileges.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Organization Owner:** no IAM role, including organization-level Owner, grants Workspace group management; it is a separate permission system.
- ✗ **B. Console is read-only:** the Groups page supports creating, editing and deleting groups for users who have the group permissions.
- ✓ **C. Group permissions come from the identity admin (correct):** the console page needs Organization Viewer, but creating groups requires Workspace or Cloud Identity group privileges that IAM roles don't provide.
- ✗ **D. Billing required:** group management is part of Cloud Identity and doesn't depend on a Google Cloud billing account.

## Key idea
Creating Google groups needs Workspace or Cloud Identity group privileges; IAM only gives access to the console page.
Q008209:
## Enabling an API is a project change
Before a Google Cloud service can be used in a project, its API must be **enabled** in that project through Service Usage. You can do it in the console (APIs & Services), with `gcloud services enable SERVICE [SERVICE ...]`, or the Service Usage API. `gcloud services list --available` shows what can be enabled.
## Required permission
Enabling needs `serviceusage.services.enable`, and disabling needs `serviceusage.services.disable`. The docs ask for the **Service Usage Admin** role (`roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin`) on the project. A project creator usually already has them through Owner.
## Similar-sounding roles
- **Service Usage Consumer**: inspect service states and **use** services (`serviceusage.services.use`), plus quota and billing consumption. It cannot enable or disable services.
- **Service Usage Viewer**: read-only view of service states.
## Example
`gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding ml-sandbox --member="user:dev@example.com" --role="roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin"`, then `gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com --project=ml-sandbox`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Browser:** it lets users browse the hierarchy and see projects and folders, with no Service Usage permissions.
- ✓ **B. Service Usage Admin (correct):** it is the documented role for enabling and disabling services and contains `serviceusage.services.enable` and `serviceusage.services.disable`, without the rest of Editor or Owner.
- ✗ **C. Project Creator:** it only allows creating new projects; it grants nothing on the services of an existing project.
- ✗ **D. Service Usage Consumer:** it lets a principal list services and call enabled ones (`serviceusage.services.use`), but it has no permission to enable or disable them.

## Key idea
To enable or disable APIs in a project, grant Service Usage Admin; Service Usage Consumer only uses already-enabled services.
Q008210:
## Disabling an API is not a cleanup
You can disable an API for a project at any time with the console or `gcloud services disable SERVICE`. What happens to existing resources depends on the service:
- **Cloud Storage and BigQuery**: data is **not deleted**, and storage keeps being billed. To stop charges, delete the data before disabling the API.
- **Cloud Run**: disabling the API **deletes** the associated Cloud Run resources.
- **Kubernetes Engine**: running clusters become **suspended**; after **30 days** suspended clusters are deleted. Re-enabling the API reactivates them, which can take up to 24 hours.
Pending fees and billable use already incurred are still charged.
## Best practice
Take an inventory of the resources that belong to a service before disabling its API (for example with Cloud Asset Inventory), and delete or migrate them deliberately.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. GKE clusters suspended then deleted (correct):** running clusters are suspended when the Kubernetes Engine API is disabled and are deleted after 30 days if it stays disabled.
- ✗ **B. Cloud Run keeps serving:** the docs warn that disabling the Cloud Run API deletes its resources, so services do not keep running.
- ✗ **C. Buckets deleted after 7 days:** there is no automatic bucket deletion; the data stays and keeps generating storage charges.
- ✗ **D. Cancels pending fees:** pending fees and billable usage are still charged after an API is disabled.
- ✓ **E. Storage data stays and is billed (correct):** disabling the Cloud Storage API doesn't touch the objects, so storage costs continue until the data is deleted.

## Key idea
Disabling an API can keep data (and its bill), delete resources (Cloud Run) or suspend them (GKE); inventory first.
Q008211:
## Metrics scopes in Cloud Monitoring
- A **resource container** (a project) stores the time-series data of its own resources.
- The **metrics scope** of a project lists the resource containers whose data that project can chart and monitor. By default it includes only the project itself.
- The project that hosts a metrics scope is its **scoping project**; it stores the alerting policies, dashboards, uptime checks and groups you create. In the console, the scoping project is the one selected in the project picker.
## Best practice
To monitor several projects together, Google recommends a **new project or one without resources** as the scoping project. If the scoping project has its own VMs, every chart and alert must filter them out, which adds complexity and room for error.
## Setting it up
In Monitoring **Settings > Metric Scope**, add projects to the scope. Changes take about 60 seconds to propagate. A metrics scope can include 375 projects by default (the quota can be raised).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Folder-level Monitoring:** there is no Monitoring switch on a folder; a metrics scope always belongs to a scoping project (even app-enabled folders use a management project's metrics scope).
- ✗ **B. Log sink to BigQuery:** log sinks route log entries, not Monitoring time series, and charts and alerting policies don't run on a BigQuery dataset.
- ✗ **C. Use shop-prod as scoping project:** it works technically, but production's own VMs then mix with staging data, the exact filtering problem the team wants to avoid.
- ✓ **D. Dedicated scoping project (correct):** an empty project whose metrics scope includes both projects can chart and alert on their data, and since it stores no metrics itself, nothing needs filtering out.

## Key idea
For multi-project monitoring, use an empty scoping project and add the monitored projects to its metrics scope.
Q008212:
## Permissions for metrics scopes
- To **view** the data that a scoping project can chart, a user needs the permissions of **Monitoring Viewer** (`roles/monitoring.viewer`) on the scoping project; nothing else.
- To **modify** a metrics scope, the user needs all permissions in **Monitoring Admin** (`roles/monitoring.admin`) on the scoping project **and** on each project being added or removed.
## Why both sides
Adding a project lets everyone who can read the scoping project see that project's metrics. Requiring admin rights on the added project means its owners agree to that exposure.
## Viewing access caution
A role with Monitoring read permission on the scoping project lets a principal see charts and alerting policies built from every project in its scope. Use separate scoping projects per team when teams should see different projects.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Logging Admin:** adding a project to a metrics scope doesn't create log sinks; it is a Cloud Monitoring setting.
- ✗ **B. Organization only:** the permission check is made on the scoping project and on each added project; no separate organization-level authorization for metrics scopes exists.
- ✓ **C. Monitoring Admin on both projects (correct):** the docs require Monitoring Admin permissions on the scoping project and on every project added to or removed from its metrics scope, so she is missing it on billing-api.
- ✗ **D. Project IAM Admin:** metrics scope membership isn't an IAM binding, and IAM administration rights don't include Monitoring permissions.

## Key idea
Changing a metrics scope requires Monitoring Admin on the scoping project and on every project you add or remove.
Q008213:
## Quotas protect capacity
Cloud Quotas limits how much of a resource a project can use. Most quotas apply per project, and many are **regional** or **zonal**: CPUs in `us-central1` are counted separately from CPUs in `europe-west1`. When a request would exceed the quota, it fails with a quota error.
## Requesting more
1. Open **IAM & Admin > Quotas & System Limits** (or the gcloud `quotas` commands).
2. Filter to the quota and the region, select it, and choose **Edit quota**.
3. Enter the new value and a justification, then submit.
Requests are mostly evaluated by automated systems, sometimes by people; you get email about the decision. Large increases can take time, so request early.
## Roles
- View quotas: Quota Viewer (`roles/servicemanagement.quotaViewer`).
- Request adjustments: Quota Administrator (`roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin`).
A paid Customer Care service is **not** required to request a quota adjustment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Paid support first:** the docs state that no paid Customer Care service is needed to request a quota adjustment.
- ✗ **B. Budget amount:** budgets only send alerts about spend; they don't set or raise quota values.
- ✗ **C. Remove location policy:** the location constraint decides where resources may be created, not how much quota a region has, and the error isn't a policy violation.
- ✓ **D. Quota adjustment request (correct):** the error is a regional allocation quota, which is raised by submitting an adjustment for that quota and region; Quota Administrator gives the permission to submit it.

## Key idea
When a quota blocks you, request an adjustment for that quota and location in Quotas & System Limits (Quota Administrator role); no paid support needed.
Q008214:
## Quotas versus system limits
- **Quotas** limit how much of a resource you can use and can usually be **adjusted** (increased or decreased).
- **System limits** are fixed constraints such as maximum file sizes or schema limits; they **can't** be changed.
## Three kinds of quotas
- **Allocation**: how much is allocated to you, such as the number of VMs; freed by deleting resources.
- **Rate**: how much you can use per time period, such as requests per minute; it **resets** when the period resets (per-day quotas at midnight Pacific Time).
- **Concurrent**: how many operations can run at once, often long-running ones.
## Scope and location
Most quotas apply at the **project** level, some at folder, organization or user level (for example, the number of projects a user can create). Quotas are also global, regional or zonal; a zonal use also reduces a regional quota if the resource has both. Quota values are specific to each project, so an adjustment in one project doesn't change others.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Zonal never counts regionally:** when a resource has both zonal and regional quotas, zonal usage reduces the regional quota shared by all zones.
- ✓ **B. System limits fixed (correct):** system limits are hard constraints of a service and can't be raised or lowered by a request.
- ✗ **C. Rate quotas need deletion:** rate quotas reset when their time period resets; deleting resources frees allocation quotas.
- ✗ **D. Identical values everywhere:** quota values are specific to each project, folder and organization; an adjustment in one project leaves others at their own values.
- ✓ **E. Per-project quotas (correct):** quotas generally apply at the project level, so one project's usage doesn't affect another project's available quota.

## Key idea
Quotas are mostly per project and adjustable; system limits are fixed; rate quotas reset with time, allocation quotas free up when resources are deleted.
Q008215:
## The quota adjuster
The **quota adjuster** watches the project's supported quotas. When peak usage approaches a quota value during a period, it tries to **increase** the value, typically by around 10-20%, and the increase is approved if possible.
- It only requests **increases**, never decreases, and doesn't touch quotas with a manual quota cap.
- It needs enough **usage history** to make accurate predictions, so the option appears only for projects (or folders, organizations) with enough activity.
- It doesn't support every quota; when a service adds support, the adjuster starts managing those quotas automatically.
- You can still file manual requests at any time.
## Alerts versus automation
A Cloud Monitoring alert on quota usage tells people they are close to a quota; it doesn't change the quota. Combining an alert with the adjuster is common.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Quota adjuster (correct):** it is the built-in feature that monitors supported quotas and requests increases automatically when usage approaches them, and the project's year of history makes it eligible.
- ✗ **B. Organization override via folder:** moving a project under a folder doesn't raise its project quotas, and organization-level overrides aren't driven by folder usage.
- ✗ **C. Set every quota to the maximum:** higher values still go through review, are often denied without justification, and can let runaway usage cost money.
- ✗ **D. Alerting policy:** alerting policies notify channels such as email or Pub/Sub; they don't submit quota adjustment requests by themselves.

## Key idea
Use the quota adjuster to request quota increases automatically as usage grows; alerts only notify.
Q008216:
## Two ways to get an organization
- **Google Workspace or Cloud Identity**: sign up, verify a DNS domain, and the organization resource is created automatically; the super admin then assigns Organization Administrator.
- **Standalone organization**: no Cloud Identity needed. New Free Trial Google Cloud customers who sign up with a Google email get a standalone organization automatically when they sign in to the console and accept the terms. It isn't available for existing Google Cloud accounts.
## Roles in a standalone organization
The account owner receives:
- `roles/cloudowner.admin` (**Organization Owner**), managed outside IAM on the **Organization details** page: add or remove owners, assign Organization Administrator, recovery contact, lifecycle.
- `roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin` (**Organization Administrator**): allow and deny policies, granting roles, viewing the hierarchy, but not creating folders or projects.
## Naming
The default name is the username plus `-org` (for example `lara-brown-org`); it can't be a domain name and can be renamed later.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Support case:** the standalone organization is provisioned automatically; no request is involved.
- ✗ **B. Domain and Cloud Identity required:** that is the classic path, but standalone organizations exist precisely so a domain and Cloud Identity aren't needed.
- ✗ **C. Folders under No organization:** folders require an organization resource, and projects can't contain folders.
- ✓ **D. Standalone organization (correct):** new Google Cloud customers get an organization resource without Cloud Identity or a domain, created at first sign-in, with the account owner as Organization Owner.

## Key idea
New Google Cloud customers without a domain get a standalone organization automatically, owned through the Organization Owner role.
Q008217:
## Organization Owner in standalone organizations
The **Organization Owner** role (`roles/cloudowner.admin`) is managed **outside IAM**, on the console's **Organization details** page. Owners can assign Organization Administrator, act as recovery contact and control the organization's lifecycle (delete, restore, rename).
## Adding owners
- An owner selects **Add organization Owner** and enters the principal. Google sends an invitation email; the principal must **accept within 30 days**.
- Owners can be individual Google Accounts or **principals in a workforce pool**, entered as `principal://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL_ID/subject/SUBJECT`. A workforce user who accepts is also granted Organization Administrator automatically.
- Each standalone organization must always keep **at least one active Google Account** as an owner.
- **Service accounts can't be invited** as owners.
## Why several owners
Multiple owners are one of the stated benefits of standalone organizations: they avoid a single point of failure when an employee leaves.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Workforce pool principal (correct):** standalone organizations accept federated workforce users as owners, identified by their workforce pool principal identifier.
- ✗ **B. Organization Administrator grants owner via IAM:** the Organization Owner role is managed outside IAM; owners are added by existing owners from the Organization details page.
- ✗ **C. Service account owner:** the docs state that service accounts can't be invited to become organization owners.
- ✗ **D. Single owner only:** multiple owners are supported and are recommended to avoid a single point of failure.
- ✓ **E. 30-day invitation (correct):** the new owner is added only when they accept the invitation, and it expires if not accepted within 30 days.

## Key idea
Standalone organizations support several owners (people or workforce pool users) added by invitation within 30 days; service accounts can't be owners.
Q008218:
## The default network
Unless disabled, every new project starts with a **default network**: an **auto mode** VPC network with one subnet per region and pre-populated IPv4 firewall rules (such as `default-allow-internal`, SSH and RDP).
- Auto mode subnets use predefined ranges inside `10.128.0.0/9`, and new regions get subnets automatically.
- That range is part of RFC 1918 space and often overlaps with on-premises networks. Auto mode networks also can't be connected to each other with VPC Network Peering or Cloud VPN, because their ranges are the same.
## Custom mode for production
Custom mode networks create no subnets automatically; you choose regions and ranges. Google calls them more flexible and better suited to production. You can convert auto mode to custom mode, but not the reverse.
## Skipping the default network
The boolean constraint `compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation` skips creating the default network and its related resources when a project is created. Set on a folder, it applies to every project created below it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Delete default firewall rules:** firewall rules don't define the network type; the auto mode network and its overlapping subnets would remain.
- ✗ **B. Convert to auto mode:** the default network is already auto mode, and conversion only goes from auto mode to custom mode, never the reverse.
- ✓ **C. skipDefaultNetworkCreation on the folder (correct):** projects created in the Production folder start with no network, so the team builds custom mode VPCs with ranges that don't collide with 10.128.0.0/16.
- ✗ **D. Keep and peer the default network:** overlapping ranges can't be routed between networks, and the default network's 10.128.0.0/9 subnets collide with the on-premises range.

## Key idea
Use `compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation` so production projects start without the auto mode default network, then build custom mode VPCs.
Q008219:
## Not every product is everywhere
Google Cloud resources live in **regions** (independent geographic areas) made of **zones** (deployment areas such as `us-central1-a`). Product availability differs: machine series, GPUs and TPUs are available only in specific zones, while some resources (images) are global and others (static external IPs) are regional.
## Checking availability for Compute Engine
- `gcloud compute machine-types list` lists machine types with the zone each is offered in. Filtering by name shows every zone (and so every region) where a machine type exists.
- `gcloud compute zones list` and `gcloud compute regions list` list locations themselves, with status.
- `gcloud compute regions describe REGION` shows a region's details, including its regional quotas.
- `gcloud compute accelerator-types list` lists GPU types by zone.
## Example
`gcloud compute machine-types list --filter="name=c4d-standard-4"` returns one row per zone that offers the type, such as `us-central1-a` or `europe-west4-b`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. regions describe:** it takes a region name such as `us-central1` and shows that region's details and quotas, not where a machine type exists.
- ✓ **B. machine-types list with a name filter (correct):** the command returns the machine type once per zone that offers it, which directly shows where c4d-standard-4 is available.
- ✗ **C. accelerator-types list:** it lists GPU accelerator types per zone, not general-purpose machine types.
- ✗ **D. zones list:** it lists zone names and status; filtering zones by a machine type name matches nothing.

## Key idea
Check machine type availability per zone with `gcloud compute machine-types list --filter="name=TYPE"`.
Q008220:
## Cloud Asset Inventory
Cloud Asset Inventory is a global metadata inventory of Google Cloud resources and policies. You can **search**, **list**, **export** and **monitor** assets in a project, folder or organization. Change history is kept for **35 days**.
## Search
`gcloud asset search-all-resources --scope=SCOPE --query=QUERY --asset-types=TYPES` searches resources interactively:
- `--scope` is `projects/ID`, `folders/ID` or `organizations/ID`.
- `--asset-types` limits results, for example `compute.googleapis.com/Instance`.
- For labels, a query value of a single `*` is an existence check: `labels.env:*` finds resources that have an `env` label.
## Other operations
- `gcloud asset export` writes a snapshot to Cloud Storage (`--output-path`) or BigQuery (`--bigquery-table`) for later analysis.
- Feeds send change notifications to Pub/Sub.
The Cloud Asset Inventory API must be enabled in the project you run the commands from.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. projects list:** it filters projects by their own labels, not the VMs inside them.
- ✗ **B. compute instances list:** it works on one project at a time and `--project` takes a project ID, not an organization ID.
- ✗ **C. asset export:** it writes a snapshot file to Cloud Storage that must then be processed, which the team explicitly doesn't want.
- ✓ **D. Organization-scope asset search (correct):** one command searches every project in the organization for VM assets, and `labels.cost-center:*` matches any VM that has the label, with results returned directly.

## Key idea
Use `gcloud asset search-all-resources` with an organization scope for quick cross-project searches; use export for bulk analysis.
Q008221:
## Ways to use Cloud Asset Inventory
- **Search**: point-in-time queries of resources and IAM policies.
- **Export**: snapshots to BigQuery or Cloud Storage for analysis with SQL or other tools.
- **History**: create, update and delete history for up to 35 days, queried on demand.
- **Feeds**: real-time notifications of changes, published to **Pub/Sub**.
## Feeds
`gcloud asset feeds create FEED_ID --organization=ORG_ID --content-type=iam-policy --asset-types=... --pubsub-topic=projects/P/topics/T` monitors resources, IAM policies, access policies or organization policies in an organization, folder or project. The first message on the topic is a welcome message; each later message describes the changed asset (a `TemporalAsset`). Conditions can narrow which changes are sent.
## Content types
`IAM_POLICY` returns the IAM bindings of an asset; `RESOURCE` returns the resource metadata; `ORG_POLICY` returns organization policies.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Daily export to BigQuery:** snapshot comparison finds changes up to a day late, which isn't near real time.
- ✗ **B. Asset history notifications:** history is queried on demand and doesn't send notifications to Essential Contacts.
- ✓ **C. Organization feed to Pub/Sub (correct):** a feed with the IAM policy content type pushes a message for every allow policy change across the organization, which a subscriber can review in near real time.
- ✗ **D. Hourly search-all-iam-policies:** this polls current state; changes made and reverted between runs are missed, and nothing is pushed per change.

## Key idea
For real-time change notifications, create a Cloud Asset Inventory feed that publishes to Pub/Sub; use export and search for analysis.
Q008222:
## What Gemini Cloud Assist is
Gemini Cloud Assist is the AI assistant built into the Google Cloud console (the Cloud Assist panel) and other surfaces. Besides general questions, it can **inspect your environment**: list resources and their configuration, recent changes, and who holds a role, and it shows an equivalent query you can run yourself to verify the answer.
## Setup from the docs
1. Enable the **Gemini Cloud Assist API**: `gcloud services enable geminicloudassist.googleapis.com` (this also enables the Gemini for Google Cloud API).
2. Enable other required APIs, including **Cloud Asset Inventory**: `gcloud services enable cloudasset.googleapis.com designcenter.googleapis.com appoptimize.googleapis.com apphub.googleapis.com`.
3. Grant users **Gemini Cloud Assist User** (`roles/geminicloudassist.user`) **and Cloud Asset Viewer** (`roles/cloudasset.viewer`), plus roles for products they need help with.
## Why Cloud Asset Viewer
Resource questions are answered from asset metadata, so the user needs read access to Cloud Asset Inventory in addition to the assistant role.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Cloud Asset Viewer and the Cloud Asset Inventory API (correct):** the documented setup pairs Gemini Cloud Assist User with Cloud Asset Viewer and enables the Cloud Asset Inventory API, which the assistant uses to answer resource questions.
- ✗ **B. Organization Administrator:** managing IAM is unrelated to reading asset metadata, and the role would be a large over-grant.
- ✗ **C. Standalone organization:** Gemini Cloud Assist works in any project where it's set up; the organization type has no effect.
- ✗ **D. Service Usage Consumer:** it lets a principal use enabled APIs, but it doesn't grant read access to asset metadata.

## Key idea
For Gemini Cloud Assist to analyze resources, enable the Cloud Asset Inventory API and grant Cloud Asset Viewer alongside Gemini Cloud Assist User.
Q008223:
## Federation without synchronization
**Workforce Identity Federation** lets users from an external IdP (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, AD FS and others supporting **OIDC or SAML 2.0**) sign in to Google Cloud with SSO. It **doesn't store user accounts** in Google Cloud, so it is **sync-less**: no Cloud Identity accounts and no Google Cloud Directory Sync.
## Building blocks
- **Workforce identity pool**: created at the **organization** level (`gcloud iam workforce-pools create POOL_ID --organization=ORG_ID --location=global`), groups identities such as employees or partners.
- **Provider**: describes the trust with the IdP (`gcloud iam workforce-pools providers create-oidc` or `create-saml`), with attribute mappings like `google.subject` and `google.groups` and optional attribute conditions.
- **Allow policies**: grant roles to pool principals.
Federated users sign in through the console (federated) and gcloud.
## Not to be confused with
**Workload** Identity Federation federates **workloads** (applications, CI pipelines), not people.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Workload Identity Federation:** it is meant for workloads, and sharing one service account among people removes per-user identity and audit trails.
- ✓ **B. Workforce Identity Federation (correct):** a workforce pool with an Okta provider gives users SSO to the console and gcloud while keeping identities in Okta, with no accounts synced into Cloud Identity.
- ✗ **C. Manual Cloud Identity accounts:** this creates the accounts the company wants to avoid, and 2-Step Verification doesn't make Google reuse Okta passwords.
- ✗ **D. GCDS plus SAML SSO:** this is a valid design, but it creates and synchronizes Cloud Identity accounts, which the company wants to avoid.

## Key idea
For people signing in with an external IdP without syncing accounts, use Workforce Identity Federation; Workload Identity Federation is for applications.
Q008224:
## Principals from a workforce pool
Federated users have no Google Account email, so allow policies refer to them by **principal identifiers** based on the pool:
- One user: `principal://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL_ID/subject/SUBJECT` (the value mapped to `google.subject`).
- All users in an IdP group: `principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL_ID/group/GROUP_ID` (from `google.groups`).
- All users with an attribute value: `principalSet://.../workforcePools/POOL_ID/attribute.ATTRIBUTE/VALUE`.
- Everyone in the pool: `principalSet://.../workforcePools/POOL_ID/*`.
## Group access caution
Every member of a mapped group gets the access, so only authorized people should be able to change membership of those groups in the IdP.
## Example
`gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding ops-tools --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/corp-pool/group/sre-team" --role="roles/compute.viewer"`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Whole pool wildcard:** this grants the role to every identity in corp-pool, far more than the SRE team.
- ✓ **B. principalSet with /group/ (correct):** the group form of the identifier matches every federated user whose `google.groups` attribute contains sre-team, exactly the required audience.
- ✗ **C. group:** email: workforce pool groups aren't Google groups with email addresses, and `iam.gserviceaccount.com` is the service account domain.
- ✗ **D. principal with /subject/:** this names a single user whose subject is the literal value sre-team, not the members of a group.

## Key idea
Grant roles to federated groups with `principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/locations/global/workforcePools/POOL/group/GROUP`.
Q008225:
## How kubectl talks to GKE
`kubectl` is the standard Kubernetes command-line tool. You can install it as a Google Cloud CLI component (`gcloud components install kubectl`); Cloud Shell already has it.
kubectl does not log in to GKE by itself. It relies on an **authentication plugin**, `gke-gcloud-auth-plugin`, which uses the client-go credential plugin framework to hand kubectl short-lived tokens based on your gcloud identity. Without the plugin, kubectl and other Kubernetes clients cannot talk to GKE clusters and show an error.
## Setup on a new machine
- `gcloud components install kubectl`
- `gcloud components install gke-gcloud-auth-plugin` (or the `google-cloud-cli-gke-gcloud-auth-plugin` package with apt or yum); check with `gke-gcloud-auth-plugin --version`
- `gcloud container clusters get-credentials CLUSTER --location=LOCATION` to write the kubeconfig entry

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Install gke-gcloud-auth-plugin (correct):** the error names a missing binary, and the plugin is what turns her gcloud credentials into tokens for kubectl; once it is installed the existing kubeconfig entry works.
- ✗ **B. Service account key file:** a key file is not a kubeconfig, and long-lived keys are a security risk to avoid; the fix is the auth plugin, not another credential.
- ✗ **C. Recreate with client certificates:** rebuilding a cluster to work around a missing local binary is disruptive, and the supported path for GKE is the auth plugin.
- ✗ **D. Grant roles/container.admin:** an IAM role adds permissions, but kubectl still cannot obtain any token without the plugin, so the same "not found" error remains.

## Key idea
kubectl on a new machine needs two gcloud components, kubectl and gke-gcloud-auth-plugin, plus get-credentials for each cluster.
Q008226:
## Two modes of GKE
- **Autopilot**: Google manages the infrastructure, including nodes, scaling, security settings and upgrades. You deploy Kubernetes manifests and GKE provisions compute to fit them. Autopilot clusters are always **regional** and always enrolled in a release channel. It is the recommended way to use GKE.
- **Standard**: you create and manage nodes in **node pools** (machine types, autoscaling, upgrades), with full control and optional zonal or regional placement.
## Billing in Autopilot
General-purpose Autopilot Pods use a **Pod-based billing model**: you pay for the resources your Pods request. Pods that select specific hardware (a machine series, GPUs) use a node-based model instead, paying for the hardware plus a management premium.
## Choosing
Small team, no wish to manage nodes, pay for what Pods ask for → Autopilot. Need for direct control of node pools and node configuration → Standard.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. MIG with Container-Optimized OS:** this drops Kubernetes altogether, so the team would build its own scheduling, service discovery and rollouts on VMs it manages.
- ✗ **B. Regional Standard with autoscaler:** three node pools are more node management, not less, and billing is still for node VMs rather than Pod requests.
- ✗ **C. Zonal Standard with auto-repair:** auto-repair and auto-upgrade help, but the team still sizes and owns the node pool and pays for the node VMs whether Pods use them or not.
- ✓ **D. GKE Autopilot (correct):** Google creates, scales, upgrades and repairs the nodes, and general-purpose Pods are billed on the resources they request, which matches both of the founders' wishes.

## Key idea
No node management + pay for what Pods request → GKE Autopilot; full control of node pools → GKE Standard.
Q008227:
## Autopilot at a glance
GKE Autopilot is a mode of operation in which Google manages the infrastructure configuration: nodes, scaling, security settings and upgrades.
- **Location**: pre-configured as regional. A regional cluster runs multiple control plane replicas in several zones of the region.
- **Nodes**: Google provisions nodes from your manifests; you request special hardware through ComputeClasses instead of creating node pools.
- **Upgrades**: every Autopilot cluster is enrolled in a release channel (Rapid, Regular, Stable or Extended; Regular by default).
- **Billing**: general-purpose Pods use Pod-based billing; Pods that select specific hardware such as GPUs or a machine series use node-based billing (hardware plus a management premium).
## Not changeable later
The availability type is fixed at creation: a zonal cluster can't become regional, and a regional cluster can't become zonal.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pod-based billing for GPUs:** Pods that select specific hardware such as GPUs use node-based billing, paying for the hardware plus a node management premium.
- ✗ **B. Zonal and convertible:** Autopilot has no zonal option, and no GKE cluster can switch between zonal and regional after creation.
- ✓ **C. Always regional (correct):** Autopilot's location setting is pre-configured as regional, so the control plane is replicated across zones in the chosen region.
- ✗ **D. Opt out of release channels:** all Autopilot clusters are enrolled in a release channel; you can pick the channel (Rapid, Regular, Stable or Extended) and use maintenance windows and exclusions, not opt out.
- ✓ **E. Google manages nodes (correct):** in Autopilot, Google provisions worker nodes for your workloads; you state hardware needs in ComputeClasses rather than building node pools.

## Key idea
Autopilot: always regional, Google-managed nodes, always in a release channel; Pod-based billing for general-purpose Pods only.
Q008228:
## Zonal and regional control planes
- A **zonal cluster** has a single control plane in one zone. If that zone has an outage, you cannot manage the cluster (deploy, scale, change config) until it returns, even if nodes in other zones keep running.
- A **regional cluster** has multiple control plane replicas spread across zones in one region, so it survives a zone loss. By default each node pool is also replicated across three zones.
Google's guidance: use regional clusters for production; for development, a regional control plane with zonal node pools costs the same as a zonal cluster.
## Fixed at creation
The availability type cannot be updated: a zonal cluster can't become regional and the reverse. Changing it means a new cluster and a workload migration.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Update with --region:** there is no in-place conversion; the docs state that a zonal cluster can't become a regional cluster.
- ✗ **B. Node pool in another zone:** multi-zonal nodes keep workloads running, but the single zonal control plane still has no replica outside us-central1-a.
- ✗ **C. Node auto-repair:** auto-repair replaces unhealthy nodes; it does nothing for the control plane and never moves it to another zone.
- ✓ **D. New regional cluster and migration (correct):** only a regional cluster replicates the control plane across zones, and because the type is fixed at creation the team must build one and move the workloads.

## Key idea
Control plane must survive a zone loss → regional cluster; zonal vs regional is chosen at creation and cannot be changed.
Q008229:
## Private nodes
With `--enable-private-nodes`, GKE creates nodes with **only internal IP addresses**. Nodes then have limited access to Google Cloud APIs and services and no route to the internet by themselves.
- **Private Google Access** is enabled automatically (unless you use Shared VPC), so nodes can still reach Google APIs such as Artifact Registry.
- For **outbound internet access** (public registries, partner APIs) you add **Cloud NAT**, which lets VMs without external IPs open connections out without accepting inbound ones.
## Other controls that sound similar
- **Authorized networks** limit which source IP ranges may reach the cluster's **control plane** IP-based endpoint. They do not affect node egress.
- `--no-enable-private-nodes` provisions nodes with external IP addresses.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Private nodes plus Cloud NAT (correct):** private nodes have no external IPs, which satisfies the policy, and Cloud NAT gives them the outbound path to the public registry and the partner API.
- ✗ **B. Public nodes with deny ingress:** --no-enable-private-nodes gives every node an external IP, which the policy forbids no matter what firewall rules are added.
- ✗ **C. Authorized networks:** they restrict who can reach the control plane endpoint; they give nodes no route to the internet.
- ✗ **D. Private Google Access alone:** it lets internal-only VMs reach Google APIs and services, not arbitrary internet hosts, so the public registry and partner API stay unreachable.

## Key idea
No external IPs on nodes → private nodes; outbound internet from them → Cloud NAT; Google APIs → Private Google Access.
Q008230:
## Deploying an image to GKE
1. **Deployment**: `kubectl create deployment NAME --image=IMAGE` creates a Deployment whose Pods run the image. The Deployment keeps the desired number of Pods running and replaces failed ones.
2. **Service**: Pods are not reachable from outside the cluster by default. `kubectl expose deployment NAME --type LoadBalancer --port 80 --target-port 8080` creates a Service of type `LoadBalancer`; GKE provisions a Google Cloud load balancer with an external IP.
- `--port` is the port clients use on the Service (80 here).
- `--target-port` is the port the container listens on (8080 here).
3. `kubectl get service NAME` shows the external IP once the load balancer is ready.
## Service types
- `ClusterIP` (default): a stable internal IP reachable only from inside the cluster.
- `NodePort`: a port on every node's IP.
- `LoadBalancer`: a network load balancer IP in front of the Service.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bare Pod with ClusterIP:** a single Pod is not recreated if it fails, and a ClusterIP Service is reachable only inside the cluster, not from the internet.
- ✗ **B. ClusterIP with ports swapped:** the Service is internal only, and the ports are reversed, sending traffic to port 80 where nothing listens.
- ✓ **C. Deployment plus LoadBalancer Service (correct):** create deployment runs and maintains the Pods, and expose with --type LoadBalancer maps public port 80 to container port 8080 through an external load balancer.
- ✗ **D. port-forward from a laptop:** port-forward tunnels traffic to her own machine for debugging; it does not publish the app to internet users.

## Key idea
Run an image on GKE with a Deployment; publish it with a LoadBalancer Service, --port for clients and --target-port for the container.
Q008231:
## Deploying from source
`gcloud run deploy SERVICE --source .` deploys a Cloud Run service straight from a source folder:
- If the folder has a **Dockerfile**, it is used for the build.
- If not, **Google Cloud's buildpacks** detect the language (Node.js, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, PHP), fetch dependencies and build a production-ready image on a Google-managed base image.
- The build runs on **Cloud Build**, so Docker is not needed locally and you don't run `gcloud builds submit` yourself.
- The image is stored in an **Artifact Registry** repository named `cloud-run-source-deploy` in the deploy region, created automatically if missing.
## When to build yourself
Deploying from source is a convenience feature and allows limited build customization. For full control, build with `gcloud builds submit` and deploy with `gcloud run deploy --image`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mandatory manual build:** building with gcloud builds submit is an option for more control, but source deploy already runs Cloud Build for him.
- ✓ **B. gcloud run deploy --source (correct):** one command uploads the folder, Cloud Build builds it with buildpacks (no Dockerfile or local Docker needed), the image lands in Artifact Registry, and the service is deployed.
- ✗ **C. Runs files without an image:** the source upload is only the build input; Cloud Run still runs a container image built from it.
- ✗ **D. --image with a folder:** --image expects a container image URL; Cloud Run always runs container images and does not treat a local folder as one.

## Key idea
No Dockerfile, no Docker → gcloud run deploy --source . (buildpacks + Cloud Build + Artifact Registry repo cloud-run-source-deploy).
Q008232:
## Two ways to make a Cloud Run service public
By default, Cloud Run checks that every caller has `run.routes.invoke` (the Cloud Run Invoker role). To allow anonymous callers you can:
- **Disable the Invoker IAM check** (recommended): `gcloud run deploy SERVICE --no-invoker-iam-check` for a new service, or `gcloud run services update SERVICE --no-invoker-iam-check` for an existing one. Re-enable with `--invoker-iam-check`. This is the documented choice when the project is subject to the **domain restricted sharing** organization policy.
- **Grant `roles/run.invoker` to `allUsers`** (the `--allow-unauthenticated` flag does this). Domain restricted sharing blocks grants to principals outside the allowed domains, so this fails in such organizations.
## Keeping control
Administrators can stop people from disabling the check with the managed constraint `constraints/run.managed.requireInvokerIam` (not enforced by default). Changing the setting needs `run.services.setIamPolicy`, included in Cloud Run Admin.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Policy exception:** weakening an organization-wide security control for one page is heavier than needed when Cloud Run offers a setting made for this case.
- ✗ **B. allAuthenticatedUsers:** this is also a principal outside the organization's domain, so the constraint blocks it, and it would not let anonymous visitors in anyway.
- ✗ **C. Load balancer in front:** a load balancer forwards requests to the service, but Cloud Run still enforces the Invoker check, so anonymous requests are still refused.
- ✓ **D. Disable the Invoker IAM check (correct):** Cloud Run then lets every request through without an IAM binding, which is the documented recommended method and works under domain restricted sharing.

## Key idea
Public Cloud Run service under domain restricted sharing → --no-invoker-iam-check, not an allUsers binding.
Q008233:
## The Cloud Run container contract for services
A Cloud Run instance has one **ingress container** that receives requests:
- It must listen on **`0.0.0.0`**, not `127.0.0.1`, on the port requests are sent to.
- The default port is **8080**. You can configure another port; Cloud Run injects it as the **`PORT`** environment variable, so reading `PORT` keeps code and config in step.
- Requests arrive as plain HTTP/1 or gRPC: **TLS is terminated by Cloud Run**, and the container should not implement TLS itself.
## Why the laptop setup fails
`127.0.0.1` accepts connections only from inside the container, and port 5000 is not where Cloud Run sends traffic. The startup check never sees the port open, so the revision fails.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Port 443 with TLS:** Cloud Run terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP to the container, and a loopback-only listener is still unreachable.
- ✗ **B. EXPOSE 5000:** Cloud Run does not pick the port from EXPOSE; it sends requests to 8080 or the port configured on the service.
- ✓ **C. 0.0.0.0 on $PORT (correct):** binding to all interfaces on the injected PORT (8080 by default) is exactly what the contract requires, so the startup probe succeeds and requests reach Flask.
- ✗ **D.:** 127.0.0.1:8080: the right port on the wrong interface; the contract says the ingress container should not listen on 127.0.0.1.

## Key idea
Cloud Run services: listen on 0.0.0.0:$PORT (default 8080), plain HTTP; Cloud Run handles TLS.
Q008234:
## What a Cloud Run container can rely on
- **File system**: writable, but it is an **in-memory** file system. Writes use the instance's memory (and can exhaust it), and data does not persist when the instance stops. Instances do not share it.
- **TLS**: terminated by Cloud Run for HTTPS and gRPC; requests reach the container without TLS.
- **Mounts**: the supported way to attach file systems is Cloud Run's managed **volume mounts** in the service configuration. Running a mount process inside the container (NFS, Filestore, SMB/CIFS) is not supported.
- **Privileges**: privilege escalation is disabled; `sudo` and setuid binaries are not supported.
## Design consequence
Keep instances stateless: put durable data in Cloud Storage, a database or a mounted volume, and install packages at image build time, not at startup.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. TLS at Cloud Run (correct):** Cloud Run terminates TLS and proxies plain HTTP/1 or gRPC to the container, so the app needs no certificates.
- ✗ **B. mount command in startup:** mounting NFS, Filestore or SMB from inside the container is unsupported; network file systems are attached through Cloud Run volume mounts.
- ✗ **C. Shared persistent /tmp:** /tmp is part of each instance's in-memory file system; nothing is shared between instances or kept after an instance stops.
- ✗ **D. sudo at startup:** privilege escalation is disabled in Cloud Run containers, so sudo and setuid binaries don't work; install packages in the image.
- ✓ **E. In-memory file system (correct):** the contract says writes use the instance's memory and don't persist when the instance stops, so it suits scratch data only.

## Key idea
Cloud Run instances are stateless: in-memory scratch disk, TLS handled by Cloud Run, no privilege escalation, volumes only through managed volume mounts.
Q008235:
## Services versus jobs on Cloud Run
- A **Cloud Run service** runs code that answers HTTP requests at an endpoint.
- A **Cloud Run job** runs code that does its work and then exits. A job is not a web server and should not listen on a port.
## Parallel tasks
A job can run as one task or as many independent tasks (up to 10,000), executed in parallel by default:
- `--tasks` sets how many tasks each execution runs.
- Each task gets `CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX` (0 to count-1) and `CLOUD_RUN_TASK_COUNT`; your code uses them to choose its share of the data.
- `--parallelism` caps how many run at once; `--max-retries` (default 3) retries failed tasks; `--task-timeout` defaults to 10 minutes.
Run it with `gcloud run jobs execute`, on a schedule (Cloud Scheduler) or from a workflow.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Service with 50 minimum instances:** it forces the batch into an HTTP shape and keeps 50 instances allocated all day for a short nightly run.
- ✓ **B. Cloud Run job with tasks (correct):** a job fits finite work without an endpoint, and splitting it into parallel tasks that read CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX shortens the nightly run with no servers to manage.
- ✗ **C. GKE CronJob with a standing pool:** it works but leaves the team managing a cluster and paying for idle nodes between runs.
- ✗ **D. One long function call:** a single invocation processes files one after another and gains no parallelism, so it is the slowest choice.

## Key idea
Run-to-completion batch on Cloud Run → Cloud Run job; parallelize with --tasks and CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX.
Q008236:
## Cloud Run functions
**Cloud Run functions** (formerly Cloud Functions) let you deploy a single function from source; it runs as a Cloud Run service. The current docs deploy it with `gcloud run deploy`:
```
gcloud run deploy FUNCTION --source . --function ENTRYPOINT --base-image BASE_IMAGE --region REGION
```
- `--source .`: build from the folder.
- `--function`: the **entry point**, the function or fully-qualified class name in your code that Cloud Run executes.
- `--base-image`: the runtime base image (for example a Python runtime image), which receives automatic security updates.
- `--allow-unauthenticated` only if the function must be public (a webhook from outside); event-triggered functions omit it.
Existing functions created with `gcloud functions deploy` (the Cloud Functions v2 API) are still supported for backward compatibility. After deployment you can attach Eventarc triggers to the function.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Entry point from the service name:** Cloud Run does not infer the entry point from the service name; the --function flag (and a base image) is what turns a source deploy into a function.
